1.pericope_label: The word after Achan: fear not, and take the spoil

schools.summary: Gill dates the word immediately after Achan's execution, the fierceness of God's anger being turned away, and reads the sentence about Ai and her king as an order to burn the one and slay the other. Calvin takes the whole passage as a deliberate raising of courage in men lately repulsed with loss and disgrace, explains the resort to stratagem by their melted hearts, since God laid no greater burden on them than they could bear until the panic passed, and holds that he used their own exertion both to keep them from looking always for miracles and to show that his power is the same under unequal modes of acting; he treats the spoils as frankly given for a reward and the burning of the city as a concession to popular feeling, the vengeance wiping out the memory of their disgrace.

Henry finds Joshua still shaken by Achan and afraid of another like him, and lays down that only when the accursed thing is faithfully put away may we expect to hear from God to our comfort, adding that corruptions within the church weaken her guides more than oppositions from without and that treacherous Israelites are more to be dreaded than malicious Canaanites. On the spoil he contrasts Achan, who lost everything by catching at what was forbidden, with the obedient people quickly recompensed, concluding that the way to have the comfort of what God allows is to forbear what he forbids; he reads the order to take all the people as a tacit rebuke for the small detachment sent before, and holds that though visions have ceased, when public men take prudent measures for the public good God has put it into their hearts.

Clarke says the iniquity being purged there was no cause to dread another disaster, and argues at length that only thirty thousand men were employed rather than the whole host — since it would be absurd to send hundreds of thousands against a town of twelve thousand people, the spies had thought three thousand enough, Joshua had no battering-rams and could not afford a siege by famine, and a larger force before the walls would have kept the enemy inside and defeated the whole design. Wesley takes the order to include all the people as meant to give every man a share in this first spoil, the weak multitude being left behind lest they hinder the stratagem and the fighting men deserving precedency in the plunder,.

Ellicott hears in the encouragement the return of Jehovah to the host for the prosecution of the war, glosses the command as taking more than the two or three thousand of the first attempt, limits the grant to the material spoil and cattle rather than the persons, notes that Jericho was exceptional in having its goods devoted as accursed, and explains that Ai is one syllable in Hebrew and means the heap, so that its first name and its final state agree, adding that the et-Tel by Bethel is uniquely the heap of nothing in particular, which seems to fix the site. Keil and Delitzsch read the command as looking beyond Ai to the conquest of the whole land, to be carried out with the entire force rather than by detachments.

debates: How large a force was engaged. Henry, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch all take the command to mean the whole host, the last extending it to the conquest of the land generally; Clarke argues from the size of Ai, the absence of siege equipment and the logic of the ambush that only thirty thousand went out.

Why a stratagem was used at all. Calvin explains it by the panic still on the people, who could not have been brought to an open conflict without it; Clarke explains it by the want of battering-rams and by the need to draw the garrison outside the walls.

How the permission to take spoil should be read. Henry makes it the reward of the obedience Achan lacked; Calvin a frank reward of victory and a concession to feeling; Ellicott a strictly limited grant of goods and cattle, against the exceptional treatment of Jericho.
outliers: Ellicott's argument from the name, that Ai means simply the heap and that the et-Tel near Bethel is the one Tel in Palestine with no further name attached.
Henry's inference that prudent measures taken by men in public trust are God's putting it into their hearts, now that visions and oracles have ceased.
Wesley's reason for leaving the weak multitude behind, that they would have hindered the stratagem.
themes: a word after the accursed thing
spoil allowed where spoil was once forbidden
how many men marched
the heap that kept its name

3.pericope_label: The ambush sent out by night, and its orders

schools.summary: Gill has Joshua rise and go up as the Lord commanded, and fills in the mechanics of the signal — a watch set to see Israel flee and the men of Ai drawn far enough from their city in pursuit before the ambush should rise.

Henry defends the stratagem as lawful because God appointed it, insisting that no league was broken and no untruth told, since only their own counsels were concealed and only a retreat counterfeited, and that men who would not keep within their walls have no complaint against those who take the advantage; he weighs the two reconstructions of the numbers and decides for a single ambush of five thousand, accepting a disturbance in the order of the narrative; he takes Joshua conquering by yielding as a type of Christ, who seemed routed by death and rallied in his resurrection; and he praises the obedience of men who took a post of real danger and executed a retreat both disgraceful and perilous without murmuring.

Clarke objects that the order to set the city on fire probably means only kindling a fire whose smoke would signal its capture, since the spoil was to be divided and burning the place outright would have consumed everything, the five thousand having stayed to save nothing but issued out at once. Wesley holds that there were only two parties and one ambush, the five thousand being part of the thirty thousand named, and reads the opening words as Joshua and his council considering the expedition rather than the whole people marching, which would have been unnecessary and burdensome.

Ellicott grants that the question of one ambush or two cannot be settled with certainty and redirects it to Joshua's object, which was to isolate Ai front and flank while closing the communications with Bethel less than two miles behind, requiring a sufficient body from the first; he also distinguishes the word used here for the lurking-place from the word used elsewhere for the ambush, and identifies the people among whom Joshua lodged as the host at Gilgal. Keil and Delitzsch reckon the march at about fifteen miles from Gilgal by a north-westerly road, so that a detachment sent off at night could be in position west of Ai before daybreak, while Joshua approached with the rest and was to flee until the garrison had been drawn quite away.

debates: Whether there were one ambush or two. Henry sets Bishop Patrick's two-party reading against the single-ambush view and decides for one of five thousand; Wesley reaches the same conclusion from comparing the two notices; Ellicott declines to decide and argues instead from the strategic need to cut Ai off from Bethel.

Whether the whole host marched. Wesley takes the opening words as a council's resolution rather than a general muster; Henry allows that the people may have encamped before the city while only thirty thousand were engaged.
What setting the city on fire meant. Clarke argues it was a smoke-signal rather than a general conflagration, since the spoil was to be preserved for division.
outliers: Henry's principle that truth once plighted becomes a debt even to an enemy, so that a stratagem may conceal counsels but must not break a treaty.
Henry's reading of the feigned flight as a type of Christ, who conquered by seeming to be conquered.
Ellicott's philological note that the lurking-place and the ambush are named by different words.
themes: a stratagem defended
thirty thousand or five
a night march to the far side
smoke as a signal

10.pericope_label: The feigned flight, the signal, and the taking of Ai

schools.summary: Gill has Joshua muster the people early to see whether any were missing, holds that the five thousand were a second ambush set perhaps nearer the city since all the men of war had been taken and thirty thousand sent first, supposes a flag on the spear as the agreed signal, and explains how the Bethelites could join the pursuit past an ambush lying between the towns, either by another road or by being let through on purpose so that Bethel too might be emptied. Calvin doubts the whole host was called out, treats the thirty-five thousand as a distribution rather than a sum, dismisses the question whether stratagem is lawful as gross ignorance since the best commanders accomplish more by art than by violence provided pledged faith is kept, doubts the spear could have been seen from the ambush across that distance and from a valley, and holds the first fire to have been partial, since burning the spoil God had granted would be absurd.

Clarke reads the numbering as an inspection of the ranks, argues that showing the whole force would have kept the men of Ai safely behind their walls, which was the one thing to be prevented; he also takes the spear to have carried an ensign whose unfurling was the agreed sign. Wesley takes the muster for the remainder of the thirty thousand rather than all Israel, sent to see whether any had slipped away in the night, reads the notice of the five thousand as a pluperfect recapitulation, records the hour appointed between Ai and Bethel and guesses they chose the hour of their earlier success as lucky, and agrees that only part of the city was fired, enough to raise a smoke.

Ellicott identifies the ravine north of et-Tel and places the main body on the rising ground beyond it, distinguishes the wider valley Joshua entered by night as chosen to draw the garrison down the Gilgal road, argues from the Ordnance map that both bodies were employed for distinct services — the firing party in the ravine nearer Ai, the larger force in the ravine next Bethel to prevent interference — explains the success of the feint by the time Joshua allowed the enemy to read his apparent intention, and sets the outstretched spear beside Jericho, where the hand of Jehovah alone worked, as here the hand of Israel and first of all of Joshua, after the manner of Moses over Amalek. Keil and Delitzsch place the camp north of Ai with the valley between, observe that not one soldier remained in either town, and suppose Bethel came in under a treaty made in expectation of a stronger attack; they judge the raised javelin visible at a distance even without a flag, since Joshua would have stood on an eminence.

debates: Whether the five thousand were a second ambush or part of the first. Gill follows the rabbis in making them a fresh body; Wesley reads the notice as recapitulation; Calvin treats the whole as one distribution of thirty-five thousand; Ellicott, from the ground itself, argues that two distinct forces were employed for two distinct purposes.

Whether the spear could serve as a signal. Keil and Delitzsch think it visible at a distance from an eminence; Calvin doubts it could be seen from a valley and suggests the ambush rose of its own accord, while allowing the gesture its value as a badge of victory.
How much of the city was burnt at first. Calvin and Wesley both hold the fire partial, a signal only, since the spoil was granted to Israel and its destruction would have been absurd.
outliers: Clarke's tactical point that a full display of Israel's strength would have kept the garrison behind its walls and ruined the plan.
Calvin's dismissal of the question whether wiles are lawful in war, on the ground that the best commanders win more by art and counsel than by force.
Wesley's guess that Ai and Bethel fixed on the hour at which they had beaten Israel before, reckoning it lucky.
themes: an inspection before dawn
two ravines and two ambushes
the hour they thought lucky
a spear held out till evening

23.pericope_label: The slaughter, the spoil, and the king hanged

schools.summary: Gill has the king spared alive only for a more shameful death, and points out that the whole city was burnt now, the earlier fire having been set to a few houses for a signal. Calvin reads the total as meaning that all who dwelt in Ai were slain rather than that all the slain belonged to it, and inclines to include those who fell in the field; he holds that vengeance justly fell sternest on the leaders with whom the cause of destruction originated, that God delivered this king alive on purpose to make the punishment more marked, that the sunset burial proves nothing was done in tumultuous impetuosity, and that Joshua's standing aloof with his hand fastened to the spear, transferring the whole praise to God, profited more than striking down heaps of the enemy.

Henry grounds the slaughter in the sentence God had already passed on Canaanite wickedness, Israel being only the ministers of his justice, observes that the men of Bethel hastened their ruin by the very step meant to prevent it, and that those whom God will destroy he first infatuates. He finds self-denial in Joshua's keeping the inferior post of standard-bearer when courage would have carried him into the action, takes the wealth of the sinner to be laid up for the just and the spoil to have been distributed in due proportions since God is the God of order and not confusion, notes that Ai seems never to have been rebuilt, and remarks that the king's body was cast at the gate where he had sat in judgment.

Clarke refers the smiting of the city to the women, children and old men left behind, insists that Joshua was literally the standard-bearer of his army and rejects a figurative reading of the outstretched spear, marks the contrast with Jericho's spoil, and supposes the king was strangled before being hung since hanging men alive was not then customary, passing on the Greek reading of a double or forked tree. Wesley makes the raised spear a sign both to encourage the men and to direct them, has the king reserved for a more ignominious punishment, and explains that the kings were dealt with more severely than the people because their example countenanced the people's wickedness and they were the chief authors of their nation's destruction.

Ellicott contrasts the spoil of Ai, assigned to Israel, with that of Jericho, claimed for Jehovah alone, gives the Hebrew of the heap for ever together with its modern name, asks why the text says the tree and suggests the king of Jericho may have hung on the same one, and turns the hanging forward to the greater Joshua, who fulfilled the curse of God in his own person and triumphed over principalities and powers in his cross. Keil and Delitzsch explain the unlowered spear by the custom of war, that a general does not drop the signal until the conflict is to cease, and record that the body was taken down at sunset in obedience to the law, cast at the town gate, and covered with a heap of stones as Achan had been.

debates: What the twelve thousand counts. Clarke restricts the smiting of the city to the non-combatants left behind; Calvin allows that reading but prefers to include those who fell in the field, both towns being small.

What the outstretched spear was for. Clarke keeps it literal, a standard held by the general himself, and rejects the analogy with Moses' hands; Keil and Delitzsch make it the ordinary war-signal; Wesley a sign of encouragement and direction; Henry and Calvin a deliberate self-effacement transferring the glory to God.

Why the king was singled out. Wesley grounds it in the responsibility of rulers for their people's wickedness and resistance; Calvin in the justice of a sterner vengeance on leaders, and in God's purpose to make the example marked.
outliers: Henry's observation that the men of Bethel hastened their destruction by taking refuge in the stronger city.
Clarke's report of the Greek reading that the king was hanged on a double or forked tree.
Ellicott's turn from the hanged king to the greater Joshua, who bore the curse himself and triumphed in his cross.
themes: executioners of a sentence already passed
a spear that was not drawn back
spoil assigned where spoil was once forbidden
a body at the gate of judgment

30.pericope_label: The altar on Ebal, the law written, and the blessings and curses

schools.summary: Gill reports the rabbinic view that the ceremony was performed the very day Jordan was crossed, which obliges its holders to march Israel a hundred and twenty miles in a day, and lists the options for what was written on the stones — an abstract of the laws, the decalogue, or the blessings and curses. Calvin presses the chronological difficulty hardest, since one verse ends at Ai and the next opens twenty miles away with no notice of a march through hostile country, and concludes that the order of time is not observed and the passage is an episode belonging later, noting that the Greek gives it after the league of the Amorites; he treats the sacrifice as the first extraordinary one offered in the land, rejects the allegorical reading of the unhewn stones in favour of a plain intention to keep altars from becoming permanent, holds that only the substance and sanctions of the law could have been inscribed, and observes that though the priests should have been dumb the stones themselves spoke clearly; on the assembly he describes the six tribes on either mount with the ark between and explains that Joshua blessed first because God allures by sweetness, curses being added only when invitation failed, each man answering Amen and so denouncing his own punishment.

Henry remarks how surprisingly the solemnity interrupts the war, refuses to transpose it on the evidence of the maps, and reads the altar's standing on the mount of the curse as signifying that where the law gave us reason to expect a curse we have peace through Christ, who was made a curse for us; he takes the rough stone to show that God is best pleased with what is plain and natural in worship, notes that the copy was written on plaster rather than graven, since writing the law in the heart is God's prerogative, and calls it a great mercy to have the law in writing and in a known tongue. On the assembly he observes that elders and judges were not above the law's cognizance and that the poorest stranger was naturalised, a presage of kindness to the Gentiles, that every word was read without omission, and that the presence of women and little ones shows masters of families should bring their households to public worship.

Clarke renders the inscription the repetition of the law and confines it to the blessings and curses of the occasion, rejecting the Decalogue, Deuteronomy and the Pentateuch alike, and explains that the women were brought forward partly because the education of the children was chiefly entrusted to them, the children themselves witnessing so that a fear of offending God might be early impressed. Wesley denies that the command required the ceremony on the day of the crossing, since circumcision and the passover came first, draws the same lesson as Henry from the altar's standing where the curses were denounced, and asks what stones or what time would have sufficed for the five books, settling on the weightiest parts and especially the ten commandments.

Ellicott takes the opening word as a note of time rather than a connective and declines to move the transaction, since the capture of Ai had given Joshua command of the road to Shechem, no strong place lay north of Bethel, and much of the district was wooded and uncleared; he ends by noting that the law can be read from this position and heard by the whole congregation, as actual experiment has proved. Keil and Delitzsch observe that after Ai Israel had gained a footing firm enough for the Mosaic instructions to be carried out.

debates: Whether the ceremony stands in its chronological place. Calvin argues from the abrupt transition, the twenty-mile march through hostile country and the silence about it that the passage is an episode belonging later, and cites the Greek order in support; Ellicott, Henry and Keil and Delitzsch all keep it where it stands, Ellicott on the ground that Ai had opened the road to Shechem.

When the command required it to be done. Gill reports the Jewish view that it fell on the day of the crossing, with the enormous march that entails; Wesley answers that circumcision and the passover came first and that as soon as opportunity offered was enough.

What was written on the stones. Clarke confines it to the blessings and curses; Wesley to the weightiest parts and the ten commandments; Calvin to the substance and sanctions, since no stones could hold the details; Gill lists the competing opinions without deciding.
outliers: Calvin's refusal of the allegorical reading of the unhewn stones, on the ground that the law's intention was simply to keep altars from becoming permanent.
Calvin's image of the inscribed stones speaking clearly even had the priests been dumb.
Clarke's reason for the presence of the women, that the education of the children was chiefly in their hands.
Ellicott's note that the acoustics of the site have been tested by experiment.
themes: a war halted for a covenant
an altar on the mount of the curse
the law written where all could read
amen from both mountains
